job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake at eight, open my laptop in our living room in Dublin, and start with a stand-up call with the data team at a logistics company. I'm a junior machine learning engineer, so I clean data, train small models for delivery times and run experiments. I finished computer science at Trinity in the summer and I've been there since October.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that the work changes weekly and that I can try things the same day. The tiring part is that I'm always learning, and I never feel I've caught up. I share a flat with my friend Dara, who's a teacher, and in the evenings I do an open-source project on air quality data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's overhyped in the sense that it won't change everything, but it's a really good tool already. At work I'd keep using it and show colleagues how. AI is a power drill, not a carpenter, and plenty of people still can't tell the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm, because my job is about using these tools and I'm good at it. The only thing nagging me is rent in Dublin, which is huge, even with my pay. My parents back me, so I'm not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: ship my delivery-time model, learn more about deployment and monitoring, and keep working on my air-quality project. I'd save 400 euros a month toward a deposit. I'd also help the data team write guidelines for responsible tool use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a feeling of being in the right place at the right time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools every day. What's one thing you'd never let them do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything involving a person's money or safety without a human check. I let it draft, summarise and write tests, but if it's about someone's delivery wages I check every line. I've seen it be confidently wrong too many times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dara, your flatmate, about the hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the hype is mostly marketing, but the tools are real. She teaches primary school, so her job will change more slowly. I'd offer to show her how it can plan a lesson, and she'd say she'd rather not.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, not a revolution, and I'd show colleagues how to use it.
I'd help the team write **guidelines** for responsible use.
think: I'm **calm**, because my job is using these tools and I'm good at it.
My only nagging worry is Dublin **rent**, even with my pay.
do: Ship my delivery-time model and learn **deployment** and monitoring.
Save **400 euros** a month toward a deposit.
feel: **Calm**, and in the right place at the right time.

fieldNote: She treats AI as a **craft tool** and still checks outputs that touch people's pay.

steps.text: Ship the delivery-time model and learn deployment
Save 400 euros a month toward a deposit
Keep working on the air-quality open-source project

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's big, and the people who learn it first will do very well. Online I'd write about what I've seen, with real numbers. The most useful thing a graduate can do now is learn to check what the machine says, not to type faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm excited and a bit uneasy. Basic modelling and data cleaning are already half done by tools, and I think companies will hire fewer juniors. But I'm already using the tools every day, so I'd be one of the ones who keeps up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward the harder parts: system design, evaluation and talking to the business. I'd take a part-time course in MLOps and start a small blog about my air-quality work. I'd also ask to mentor the next intern, so I'm seen as useful to the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a flicker of worry. It feels like a surfing day: big waves, and you can fall off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks in your own work would software take over first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cleaning data, first-draft code, report writing. I'd take those by myself and show my manager how much faster I'm. Then I'd go to the harder questions, such as whether the model is fair to couriers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your company do about the junior roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd hire fewer, but pay the ones they keep more. I'd rather be in the group they keep. That's a bit selfish, I know, and I do feel guilty about the people who aren't.

I'd write online about what I've seen, with **real numbers**.

steps.text: Take a part-time MLOps course in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules now, and I'd say it loudly. At work I'd argue for slowing deployment where people's jobs are at stake. I'm helping build the thing, and I'm saying we should slow down and write laws first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared but also strangely ready. My field goes first, I'm sure of that, but I'd also be among the first to know how to use it. I think my pay and jobs would shift in about a year, and entry-level roles like mine would vanish before senior ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as hard as I can, maybe 900 euros a month, and put my air-quality project into a proper not-for-profit with some friends. I'd try to build a worker co-operative that runs AI systems for small firms. I'd also move back toward my parents' house if the rent goes crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with energy. It's a sleepless-night feeling, and it's also an adrenaline feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what exactly would you try to start this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd email two friends about forming the co-op and write down what we'd offer: running and checking AI for local firms. I'd also join a campaign for a worker-voice law. It's a small thing, but doing something helps me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you want your government to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want a public fund that pays for retraining and basic income pilots, rules that make companies report layoffs, and a slow-down where it's risky. I know the last one is hard, but the first two seem obvious.

say: I'd say we need **rules now** and ask to slow deployment where jobs are at stake.
I'd say it **loudly**, though I help build the technology.
think: I'm **scared but ready**: my field goes first, yet I'd know how to use it.
I expect entry-level roles like mine to vanish before **senior** ones.
do: Save about **900 euros** a month and form a not-for-profit with friends.
Plan a worker **co-operative** that runs and checks AI for small firms.
Join a campaign for a **worker-voice** law.
feel: **Alarmed**, but with adrenaline and energy rather than numbness.
S2.quote: I'm helping build the thing, and I'm saying we should slow down and write laws first.
fieldNote: She is both **builder and critic**, which makes her say and think consistent but tense.
The co-operative idea is concrete and tied to her skills.
She picks **anxious**, not alarmed: she expects work to shift but has a plan.

steps.text: Set up a worker co-operative that runs AI for small firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and I want to use it. At work I'd start the conversation about how the company shares gains with staff. If a machine does the work of five of us, the five should still get a say in where the money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious but not terrified. I think by 2031 my current role would be mostly supervising agents, and fewer people would be doing it. I could see myself running a small company that checks and audits AI for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and use my evenings to build the audit business with two friends. I'd save 600 euros a month and learn some law about AI accountability. I'd also stay active in the open-source community, because that's where my reputation is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and worried at once. Five years feels like an actual runway, so I'm mostly focused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you build that isn't just a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small business that audits AI tools for charities and councils, and that's not dependent on one employer. I'd register a company in year two, and take my first client in year three. Honestly, it's a bet, but my savings can cover a thin year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the three extra years before robots affect Dara's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dara teaches children, and robots come later for hands-on care, so she's safer than me. But I'd think about what happens to her school budget if tax income drops. That's the sort of knock-on effect that scares me.

I'd start a conversation about where the **money** goes.

I could run a small company that **audits** AI for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and I'd use it to get involved in how it's governed. Online I'd push for open-source safety tools. Ten years is long enough to build something that outlasts my job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm pretty calm. By 2036 I'd be 32 and could be running my own company or working in AI safety. I'd worry for people who don't have the skills or backing I have, though, and I'd feel that's my responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on with the job, finish a master's part-time in machine learning ethics, and put money into a flat. I'd keep the open-source project and try to turn it into a small non-profit. I'd also volunteer teaching coding at a youth club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit hopeful. A decade feels like a proper career, even if it's a strange one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years that you wouldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but more as a safety and evaluation job than a building one. I'd also like to build tools for people with little money, such as free AI helpers for renters. That's the kind of thing a ten-year window allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still do machine learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be rushing to survive. With ten I can try to make something that helps others. That's the difference between panic and purpose, I think.

I'd push for **open-source** safety tools online.
think: I'm pretty **calm**, since by 32 I could run my own company or work in AI safety.
I'd feel **responsible** for people without my skills or family backing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though I'd cope better than most. I help build this stuff, and I'd still lie awake wondering who gets left out if it moves in two years. What would help is rules made fast, retraining money and a worker voice in how firms use it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I'm lucky. I have a family that can catch me and skills in demand, and that's not true for most people. I'd like what I know to be used for people who don't have that.

headlineQuote: I help build this stuff, and I'd still lie awake wondering who gets left out if it moves in two years.
portrait: Kira is **22**, a computer science graduate working as a junior machine learning engineer for a logistics firm in Dublin.
She uses AI tools every day, has no debt and over six months saved, and her parents would back her.
She is progressive and **blames** weak regulation and firms, and she turns worry into a co-operative and open-source plan.
She moves first: audits, side projects and campaigns, and she stays aware that her own luck is **uneven**.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, because the speed leaves little time for rules and for people without her backing.
whatWouldHelp: Fast **rules**, retraining money and a worker voice in how firms use AI.
